title: Maitreyi's question
word: in their own words where they exist
hook: offered a share of the property, Maitreyi asks what wealth can't give, and Yajnavalkya teaches the Self, the atman
carry: all is dear for the sake of the self
tomorrow: a saint who signed her hymns as a ghoul.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gargi, warned not to ask too much, came back with two questions, and the answer: everything is woven on Brahman, the imperishable.

A man is about to leave home for good, to live as a wandering seeker. Before he goes, he does the responsible thing: he sits down with his wife to settle the property, so that she and his other wife will be provided for. The will, the house, the money. His wife listens. Then, instead of asking how much, she asks something else entirely. The man is Yajnavalkya again, the sage Gargi questioned. The wife is Maitreyi, whom you first met in year one.
screen: `A MAN ABOUT TO LEAVE HOME.` → `THE TALK ABOUT THE PROPERTY.` → `MAITREYI ASKS SOMETHING ELSE.`

segments.voice: The scene is in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad. Yajnavalkya tells Maitreyi he's about to leave this life at home, and wants to make a settlement between her and Katyayani, his other wife. Maitreyi answers, in paraphrase: sir, if this whole earth, filled with wealth, were mine, would I become immortal by it? No, he says. Your life would be like the life of the rich; there's no hope of immortality through wealth. Then her line: what would I do with something that won't make me immortal? Tell me what you know. She isn't refusing to be provided for. She's refusing to let the property be the whole conversation. The text has him say she is dear to him, and speaks dear words. Then he teaches. A husband is dear, he says, not for the husband's own sake, but for the sake of the Self. A wife, children, wealth, the world itself: all dear for the sake of the Self. It's the Self that must be seen, heard, thought on, and meditated upon. That Self is the atman, the deepest you, and the same Upanishad says in a famous line: this Self is Brahman. Here's the teaching. Hindus name four aims of life: dharma, what's right; artha, wealth; kama, pleasure; and moksha, freedom. Wealth is a real aim, not a sin. Maitreyi doesn't scorn it. She simply knows which aim it can't reach.
screen: `THE TALK ABOUT THE PROPERTY` · `WOULD WEALTH MAKE ME IMMORTAL?` · `DEAR FOR THE SAKE OF THE SELF` · `DHARMA · ARTHA · KAMA · MOKSHA`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you're working toward or wanting right now, a purchase, a grade, a result, and hold it gently. Hindu teachers call this kind of sorting viveka, discernment. Ask Maitreyi's question of it, without judging: what would I do with this? What can it give, and what can't it? Then turn toward whatever feels deeper than the thing itself and rest there; if you pray, bring that deeper want before God.
In their own words, where they exist. Today, Maitreyi, offered a share of the property, asking what she would do with what can't make her immortal. Today's word.
Your line: all is dear for the sake of the Self. One question, asked at the edge of a goodbye. That's today.
